Issued at 1236 PM CDT Tue Oct 20 2026

Rest of Today - Friday: Dry with Above Normal Temperatures

Rather mundane weather continues across the region over the next 
several days as tropospheric deep ridging remains the dominant 
synoptic feature across much of the United States. Rising heights 
and warm air advection associated with this ridging sets up 
favorable conditions for above normal temperatures across the Upper 
Mississippi River Valley as 850hPa temperatures top out around 9C-
11C. As a result, afternoon high temperatures top out in the mid 60s 
to low 70s through Friday while overnight lows fall into the 40s and 
50s, roughly 15-20 degrees above normal for this time of year. 
Confidence in this unusual warmth is high given very little spread 
in the 10th-90th spread of the various ensemble suites, but did 
trend the temperature forecast towards the 90th percentile of the 
NBM to account for the potential of efficient mixing and 
overachieving temperatures.

A couple chances for fog development also occur this week: Tonight-
Wednesday morning and Wednesday Night-Thursday Morning. The second 
period looks to be more favorable for widespread fog as the 850hPa 
ridge axis and light winds more directly situate over the region, 
setting up a favorable scenario for efficient radiational cooling 
and thus fog development. The 20.12z REFS already suggests 40-60% 
probabilities for visibility less than 3 miles during this 
timeframe. Tonight into Wednesday morning is slightly less favorable 
owing to stronger winds in the 925-850hPa layer, but sufficient 
cooling should be able to occur under mostly clear skies such that 
at least the more susceptible river valleys should see some 
development. Otherwise, with the ridging in place and lack of 
substantial forcing or moisture, a precipitation free forecast is in 
place through the remainder of the week.

Saturday - Sunday: Low Precipitation Potential Returns

The upper level ridge begins to break down late this week, shifting 
eastward this weekend while a 500hPa trough moves across southern 
Canada and a cutoff low develops across the southwest United States. 
In response to the approaching upper low, surface cyclogenesis 
occurs across the northern Great Plains before the mature low lifts 
northward into Canada. As this feature lifts north, a surface cold 
front looks to move through the Upper Midwest, providing some weak 
forcing for precipitation this weekend. However, timing and location 
of this boundary is a bit uncertain and the more favorable 
environment for rainfall looks to occur across central Minnesota 
where deeper moisture is currently forecast to be present. So, while 
precipitation may return this weekend, probabilities are rather low, 
around 10-30%. 

Early Next Week: Higher Forecast Uncertainty

As we head into early next week, quite a bit of uncertainty 
surrounds the forecast as deterministic and ensemble model suites 
vary significantly in their evolution of the atmosphere. Solutions 
such as the GFS/GEFS/AIGFS and Euro/EPS/AIFS suggest this weekend's 
frontal boundary stalls out across our area while another 500hPa 
trough along the United States/Canada border phases with the cutoff 
low across the Southwest, continuing eastward and sparking showers 
along said boundary on Monday. However, the Canadian/GEPS solutions 
depicts the 500hPa ridge retrograding back into the Upper Midwest 
early next week, resulting in predominantly dry conditions. Due
to these variations, low and rather nebulous precipitation 
probabilities exist for early next week, around 10-20% in the 
20.13z NBM. This uncertainty is also reflected in the 
temperature forecast as ensemble guidance has fairly large 
spreads in the 25th-75th percentiles, upwards of 10 degrees. 
However, the overall temperature trend for early next week at 
this point is towards more seasonable temperatures.
